analysis.one_liner: Requires mortgage and business lenders to report loan data by race, gender, and income to expose lending discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Banking Committee in 1989 with zero cosponsors and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have expanded a 1975 law that requires banks to disclose where they make mortgage loans. It would have forced lenders to report loan applications, not just loans they approved, and to break the numbers down by the borrower's income, race, and gender — making it possible to see who gets rejected. It also would have extended the reporting rules to every mortgage lender, not just banks, and required banks to disclose data on business loans, including small business loans.
analysis.who_benefits: Borrowers — especially minority, women, and lower-income applicants — plus the community groups, regulators, and researchers who use loan disclosure data to spot neighborhoods or groups being shut out of credit. Requiring disclosure of applications (not just loans made) would expose denial patterns for the first time in commercial lending, and extending the rules to all mortgage lenders would close the gap around non-bank lenders.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Borrowers, especially minority and low-income applicants

how_it_helps.text: Requires lenders to report the number and dollar amount of mortgage loans broken down by the borrower's income level, race, and gender, so discrimination patterns become visible in the data.

Requires lenders to disclose loan applications they received, not only loans they originated or approved — under current law, a lender could reject nearly every applicant in a neighborhood without it showing in the public record.
Extends mortgage disclosure rules to every mortgage lender, closing a loophole that let lenders outside the banking system make loans without public reporting.

Requires banks to disclose commercial loan data, itemized to show small business loans, federally guaranteed loans, and business lending broken down by income, race, and gender — information relevant to whether minority-owned and small businesses can get credit.

analysis.who_pays: Banks, savings institutions, credit unions, and all mortgage and commercial lenders, which would bear the cost of collecting, itemizing, and reporting the new data — the bill would have taken effect within 60 days of enactment, mid-year 1989. Regulators would also take on additional oversight work, and lenders would face public scrutiny of their lending records.
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and mortgage lenders, through reporting costs

drawbacks.text: The bill imposes real paperwork costs: every depository institution would have to collect and itemize data by income, race, and gender for both mortgages and, for the first time, all commercial loans — a large expansion of a law originally limited to mortgage lending.

Extending reporting to any person who originates or purchases mortgage loans pulls small, independent mortgage lenders into a federal compliance regime built for banks, with an effective date just 60 days after enactment.
Disclosure alone does not stop discrimination — it gives regulators, researchers, and community groups the evidence, but enforcement still depends on follow-up action by agencies and courts.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is accountability: loan-denial data broken down by race, gender, and income is the basic tool for detecting redlining and lending discrimination, and the bill would have closed real loopholes by covering applications, non-bank lenders, and commercial lending. The costs are compliance paperwork and public scrutiny for lenders — modest for large institutions, more burdensome for small ones. On balance the disclosure benefits outweigh the compliance costs, but the bill's speed (a 60-day effective date) and its extension into commercial lending gave opponents fair ground to call it overbroad.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Banking Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never acted on it, and it died when the 101st Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Senator Howard Metzenbaum introduced the bill on May 3, 1989, and it was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs the same day.
No other senator signed on — the bill had zero cosponsors.
No further action was ever taken: the bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote, and it expired with the 101st Congress on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks, savings institutions, and mortgage lenders came out ahead: they never had to report loan applications or lending broken down by race, gender, and income, and their lending records stayed out of the public data.

for.name: Sen. Howard M. Metzenbaum
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its only sponsor; no other senator joined him.

against.name: Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on the day it was introduced and never held a hearing, markup, or vote; the bill never left the committee.

against.name: Chair Donald Riegle
against.role: Chair, Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs
against.what_they_did: As chairman of the committee of referral, never scheduled the bill for committee action during the two-year Congress.

against.name: 0 of 55 Senate Democrats
against.what_they_did: Not one member of the Democratic majority cosponsored the bill.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and no senator besides the sponsor took any position, so the bill's partisan shape was never tested — though zero cosponsors from the 55-member Democratic majority meant the sponsor stood alone.

industries.note: The bill would have required banks to report loan applications and lending data itemized by income, race, and gender for both mortgages and commercial loans, exposing denial patterns and lending discrimination to public view. Banks' interest in avoiding this scrutiny runs directly against the borrowers and neighborhoods the data would protect.

The bill extended the Home Mortgage Disclosure Act's reporting rules to any person who originates or purchases mortgage loans, pulling independent mortgage lenders — previously outside the law — into public disclosure. Their interest in staying unreported ran against transparency for borrowers.
Regulators would have received far more detailed lending data to assess compliance with nondiscrimination requirements, but would also have shouldered the added work of collecting and reviewing it.
